opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to picture it is that the model has this residual stream, which is basically a shared vector space that every layer reads from and writes back into. An MLP neuron interacts with that space in two distinct steps.

First, there's the read side. Each neuron has an input weight vector, which you can think of as a direction in the residual stream. When a token's representation comes through, the neuron takes a dot product with that direction, so it's asking, "How much of this particular direction is present right now?" Then you apply the nonlinearity, whether that's a ReLU or a GELU or whatever the model uses. That gives you a single scalar activation that says how strongly the neuron fired.

Then there's the write side. Each neuron also has an output weight vector, which is another direction in the residual stream. The neuron takes its activation and adds that output direction back into the stream, scaled by how strongly it fired. So in effect it's saying, "I saw this pattern, so I'm going to push the representation this way."

That framing is really useful for interpretability because it lets you ask two separate questions about a neuron: what is it detecting, and what is it contributing? Sometimes those line up nicely. You might find a neuron that reads a direction meaning "we're inside a piece of code" and writes a direction that boosts tokens like closing brackets.

The catch, and this is a big part of why we've moved toward things like transcoders and sparse features, is that individual neurons are often polysemantic. Because of superposition, the model packs more concepts than it has neurons, so any given neuron's read direction might respond to several unrelated things. The read/write picture still holds mechanically, but the directions we care about conceptually often don't line up with single neurons. So a lot of the work is finding a better basis, one where each read and write direction is actually interpretable, and then you can trace how features read from earlier ones and write into later ones to build up circuits.

r001.rationale: It says the neuron takes a dot product between the representation and its input-weight direction to measure how much of that direction is present.

r002.rationale: It says the neuron scales its output-weight direction by its activation and adds that direction back into the residual stream.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I like to think about it is that a neuron is really two things glued together. There's a read direction and a write direction, and in between there's a nonlinearity.

So you have the residual stream, which is this big vector that the whole model is passing along from layer to layer. Every MLP neuron has an input weight vector, and what it does first is just take a dot product between the residual stream and that vector. That's the read. It's asking, "how much of this particular direction is present right now?" If the residual stream is pointing in a direction that's aligned with the neuron's input weights, you get a big positive number. If it's orthogonal, you get roughly zero. So the neuron is essentially probing for a feature, or really for some linear combination of features, in the current representation.

Then you hit the nonlinearity, the GELU or ReLU or whatever it is, and that's what makes it interesting, because now it's not just a projection. It's a gate. Below some threshold the neuron is quiet and it contributes nothing. Above it, it fires, and the amount it fires scales with how strongly that direction was present.

And then the write is the other half. The neuron has an output weight vector, and whatever scalar activation came out of the nonlinearity gets multiplied by that vector and added back into the residual stream. So the neuron is saying, "if I see this direction, I write that direction." And crucially the read and write directions don't have to have anything to do with each other. A neuron can read "this token is in a parenthetical" and write "boost the probability of a closing paren." The read is about detecting, the write is about acting.

Once you frame it that way, a whole MLP layer is just a few thousand of these if-then rules running in parallel, all reading from the same stream and all adding their contributions back in. And I find that framing really useful because it explains a lot of why interpretability is hard. The neuron's input direction is one thing, its output direction is another, and neither of them is guaranteed to line up neatly with a single human concept. You get superposition, you get neurons that read a mix of things and write a mix of things. But the underlying mechanic is really simple: dot product in, gate, scaled vector out.

r001.rationale: It says the neuron takes a dot product of the residual stream with its input weights to measure how much that direction is present.

r002.rationale: It says the activation is multiplied by the output weight vector and added to the residual stream, describing a write along that vector.

astra-6.text:
One useful way to think about an MLP neuron is that it has a read direction and a write direction. On the way in, it takes a dot product between the input vector and its input weights. That tells you how strongly the input aligns with the direction the neuron is looking for. You add a bias and apply a nonlinearity, and that gives you a scalar activation.

Then the neuron multiplies that scalar by its output weight vector. So it’s reading in one direction and writing in another, with the activation controlling how much it writes. In a transformer, that contribution gets added back into the residual stream, alongside the contributions from the other neurons.

That gives us two useful questions: What kind of input activates this neuron? And when it activates, what does its output do to the model’s subsequent computation? Those are distinct questions, and you need both to understand its role.

r001.rationale: It says the neuron takes a dot product with its input weights, measuring how strongly the input aligns with the direction the neuron looks for.

r002.rationale: It says the activation scales the output weight vector, so the neuron writes along that vector’s direction.

sol-6.1.text:
One useful way to think about an MLP neuron is that it reads from one direction and writes to another. Its input weights define a direction, and taking the dot product with the incoming activation tells you how strongly that direction is present. You apply a nonlinearity, which determines how much the neuron activates, and then that activation scales its output weight vector.

So the neuron is effectively saying, “When I detect this feature, add this vector to the representation.” In a transformer, that output gets added to the residual stream. And the reading and writing directions can be different: the neuron can detect one thing and contribute information that helps some later computation.

r001.rationale: It says the input-weight direction’s dot product with the incoming activation measures how strongly that direction is present.

r002.rationale: It says the neuron’s activation scales its output-weight vector, adding that vector to the representation.
